newsitem.title: GERMANY: Zwickel plan courageous, not workable-German press.
newsitem.headline: Zwickel plan courageous, not workable-German press.

text.p: A proposal by German union leader Klaus Zwickel to cut the working week to just 32 hours to create new jobs is a courageous plan, but is unlikely to achieve the desired effect of slashing unemployment, German newspapers said on Thursday.

Zwickel on Wednesday injected life into a two-day jobs conference organised by labour leaders with a surprise proposal that the working week in the engineering sector, now at 35 hours, should be cut back even further to 32 hours.
He also called for unions in other sectors, which still have longer working weeks, to seek a 35-hour week.

Editorials in leading newspapers said that while Zwickel had certainly secured headlines for the conference with his proposal, but had not presented a truly workable solution to Germany's record unemployment.

The Handelsblatt business daily said: "IG Metall is demonstrating the will to act at a time when otherwise lack of action and helplessness characterise the response to the most urgent problem facing western industrial society -- vast job losses," it added.

"But at the same time, Zwickel's proposal for a general cut in working hours is on the wrong track to resolve the employment problems....Individual, not collective regulations are the order of the day," Handelsblatt said.
The conservative daily Die Welt took a similar tone.
"With his surprise push to achieve a 32-hour week, the IG Metaller has taken the initiative and declared to all unions where the road is taking them," it said.
"Without doubt (this) gave considerable drive to a jobs summit which otherwise appeared rather weary. But the debate about more jobs has scarcely been taken decisively further.

"Even a cut in the working week without total wage compensation does not offer a way out of mass unemployment," Die Welt said, pleading instead for greater deregulation to allow a greater number of low-wage jobs to be added.
The Frankfurter Rundschau described Zwickel's move as "a huge, daring step".
Yet it added that it was not clear how much support there was for the proposal. "The attempt is daring and courageous. But the jury is still out on who will share the burden."
But the Sueddeutsche Zeitung diverged from the general consensus to take a more negative tone on the jobs summit.
"No more emerged from this than the mutual confirmation of all participants that the situation on the German labour market front is really very serious," the Sueddeutsche said.

"But at least unions, politicians and industrialists did this together, after a long period of radio silence," it said, adding, "It is nonetheless frustrating that the unions are still turning round the old prayer wheel of shorter working hours."
